content: Snuff, a form of smokeless tobacco, is traditionally understood as dry or European nasal snuff. It is available in various types and is used in different ways. Dry snuff is often scented or flavored, with options ranging from floral, mentholated (also referred to as medicated), fruity, and spicy, either as single flavors or blends. A German variety called Schmalzler is typically moist and milder compared to standard dry snuff. Dry snuff also varies in texture and moisture levels, from very fine to coarse, and from toast (extremely dry) to very moist. Generally, finer snuff tends to be drier. Common flavors include spearmint, cinnamon, raspberry, orange, rose, menthol and camphor, whiskey, bourbon, and tonka bean. Several brands of dry snuff exist, including Bernard Brothers (founded in 1733), Lotzbeck (1774), Sternecker (1900), Pöschl (1902, makers of Gawith Apricot), Wittmann (1955), Arnold Andre, Dallmayr, Gletscher Prise, Fribourg & Treyer (1720), Wilsons of Sharrow (1737), Samuel Gawith (1792), Gawith Hoggarth (1854), Hedges, McChrystal's, Toque Tobacco Ltd. (2006), De Kralingse, L. Dingler, Swedish Match, Dholakia, M/s Bhogilal Mafatlal & Sons, and P.V. Rajan & Company. American snuff, in contrast to European snuff, is moist and is typically applied to the gums rather than inhaled. Known as dipping tobacco, it is similar to Swedish snus. American snuff comes in sweet and salty varieties, with additional flavors like peach, mint, and licorice. Dipping tobacco is distinct from chewing tobacco. In India, creamy snuff is a paste made of tobacco, clove oil, glycerin, spearmint, menthol, and camphor, sold in toothpaste-like tubes. It is marketed primarily to women under brand names such as Ipco (produced by Asha Industries), Denobac, Tona, and Ganesh. Snuff accessories were once a lucrative industry, especially when snuff-taking was fashionable. In Europe, snuff boxes ranged from simple materials like horn to highly ornate designs made with precious materials and advanced techniques. Large communal snuff containers, called mulls, were often kept on tables. A famous silver communal snuff box at the British House of Commons was destroyed during World War II. In China, snuff bottles were used, often made of glass with intricate internal decorations or layered multi-colored glass, where parts of the layers were removed to create images. Historically, snuff-taking was first documented among Native Americans by a monk named Ramon Pane in 1493 during Columbus's second voyage to the Americas. In 1561, Jean Nicot, the French ambassador in Lisbon, sent snuff to Catherine de' Medici to treat her son's migraines, leading to her becoming an enthusiast. By the 1600s, some opposed snuff use. Pope Urban VIII threatened excommunication for snuff-takers, and in 1643, Tsar Michael of Russia imposed the punishment of nose removal for snuff use. Despite this, snuff had notable supporters, including King Louis XIII of France, and by 1638, its use had spread to China. By the 1700s, snuff became the preferred tobacco product, with enthusiasts like Napoleon, Queen Charlotte (wife of George III), and Pope Benedict XIII. The 1700s also saw the first warnings about tobacco, with English doctor John Hill cautioning against excessive snuff use due to its association with nasal cancers. The U.S. federal tax on tobacco was introduced in 1794. Snuff-taking etiquette historically reflected social status. Rules included refraining from taking snuff in the presence of women unless in informal settings like public houses. Women were traditionally expected to abstain from tobacco until at least 50 years of age. Snuff boxes were chosen based on the occasion, with materials like silver, ivory, or mother-of-pearl suitable for formal events, while brass or teak was appropriate for casual settings. Pewter was avoided due to its softness, and snuff pouches were unsuitable as they could make the snuff too moist. Napoleon, for instance, was distressed when a fragile mother-of-pearl snuff box gifted by Empress Josephine broke, until she replaced it. Proper snuff-taking involved specific steps: transferring the snuff box to the left hand, tapping it to gather the powdered tobacco, inspecting the contents, and presenting it to others with a courteous bow. The snuff box was passed clockwise and held in the left hand. A pinch of snuff was taken with the right hand, held briefly between the fingers, and then brought to the nose without leaning forward. The head was slightly tilted back, and snuff was inhaled with precision through both nostrils without grimacing or sneezing. Sneezing was considered rude in Britain, though acceptable in Europe. Snuff should not enter deeply into the sinuses. A method involving the anatomical snuffbox (a thumb indentation) was discouraged due to the risk of spillage. After use, the snuff box was closed with a flourish and returned to the jacket pocket. The nose and collar were wiped with a handkerchief, often colorful and disposable due to rapid soiling. Sneezing in public without a handkerchief was frowned upon. Legally, oral snuff, such as dipping tobacco and snus, is banned in most of the European Union, except in Scandinavia, where snus remains popular. Snuff is widely available over the counter in most European tobacco shops. In Britain, snuff is significantly cheaper than cigarettes and other tobacco products as it is tax-exempt, though it still carries the same duty-free limitations as other tobacco products.
